title: Daily low‐dose aspirin and blood pressure in community‐dwelling older adults

sections.abstract: High‐quality randomized trial evidence is lacking on whether low‐dose aspirin exerts significant effects on blood pressure (BP) in older adults. The authors assessed longitudinal BP changes in participants enrolled in ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE), a randomized, placebo‐controlled trial of 100 mg daily aspirin in 19 114 community‐dwelling Australian and U.S. adults without cardiovascular disease (CVD), dementia, or independence‐limiting physical disability. Participants’ BP was recorded at baseline and annual study visits, and managed by their usual care provider. BP trajectories for aspirin versus placebo during 4.7 years of follow‐up were examined for systolic and diastolic BP separately, using linear mixed models to account for between and within‐individual variability in BP. Analyses by subgroups were also explored with inclusion of interaction terms in the models. The difference in mean change in systolic BP between aspirin and placebo during study follow‐up was −0.03 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.13, 0.07; p = .541) (aspirin minus placebo), while the mean difference for change in diastolic BP was −0.05 mm Hg (95% CI: –0.11, 0.01; p = .094). These small, non‐significant differences in BP change between the aspirin and placebo groups were consistent across baseline levels of BP and antihypertensive treatment status (treated/untreated). Likewise, subgroups of age, sex, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and frailty revealed no interaction effect between the subgroup, aspirin treatment, and time. Interval‐censored Cox proportional hazards regression showed no difference in rates of incident treated hypertension between aspirin and placebo‐treated participants. The authors conclude that daily low‐dose aspirin does not significantly affect BP in older adults when managed by usual care.
sections.introduction:
High blood pressure (BP) is an important modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD). Despite the availability of numerous inexpensive and highly effective antihypertensive drugs, more than half of individuals with hypertension have BP that is uncontrolled. 1 Small changes in BP in either direction can have marked impact on CVD risk; therefore, assessment of BP should include a careful consideration of the potential contributing effects of accompanying medications which may affect BP.

Nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), are widely available without prescription and are among the most frequently used drugs, especially in older adults, to treat conditions involving pain and inflammation. These agents exert their pharmacologic effects by inhibiting the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes responsible for production of prostaglandins regulating homeostatic functions such as gastric protection, maintenance of renal blood flow, and platelet activation and aggregation. However, NSAIDs have the potential to increase BP, through their inhibition of prostaglandins E 2 (PGE2) and I 2 (PGI2) which are potent smooth muscle vasodilators, as well as by impairing the natriuresis mediated by PGE2 in the thick ascending loop of Henle and collecting duct, leading to sodium and water retention. 2

While early meta‐analyses pooling data from small trials suggested non‐significant increases in BP with short‐term use of NSAIDs in younger normotensive individuals, 3 , 4 prospective observational studies, usually grouping aspirin with other NSAIDs, reported an increased risk of hypertension with higher doses and longer term use. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 Few studies have focused specifically on aspirin's effects on BP and most assessed whether aspirin antagonized the effect of concurrent antihypertensive treatment. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 In addition, there is a series of small randomized studies from one research group suggesting that aspirin 100 mg administered at nighttime lowers BP in younger healthy patients and those with pre‐hypertension or hypertension. 14 , 15 , 16

Importantly, there remains a lack of high‐quality randomized trial evidence on whether aspirin affects BP in older adults, as they have not been sufficiently represented in prior research examining aspirin's effect on BP. This question is particularly relevant for older aged adults, where both the risk and prevalence of hypertension and its complications are significantly increased. To address this important evidence gap, we performed a post‐hoc analysis to examine the effects of daily low‐dose aspirin on BP in participants enrolled in the ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE) trial.
sections.methods:
The ASPREE trial was a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial of 100 mg daily aspirin to prolong disability‐free survival in 19 114 healthy adults aged 70 years and older in Australia and the U.S. (aged 65 years and older for U.S. minorities). 17 Briefly, participants were consented and enrolled from 2010 to 2014, and the blinded, in‐trial phase was completed in 2017. All analyses in this report were restricted to the blinded, randomized trial period. As a condition of enrollment, participants had to be without documented evidence of prior CVD, dementia, or independence‐limiting physical disability, and free of any life‐limiting illness expected to cause death within the planned 5‐year follow‐up period. Individuals with uncontrolled BP (systolic BP ≥180 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥105 mm Hg) were excluded from participation.

Recruitment occurred through community‐based general practitioners in Australia, and from academic and community medical centers and health systems in the U.S. Enrolled participants attended annual study visits for collection of study endpoints, as well as assessments of cognition, physical function measures, lifestyle, anthropometric measures, medical history, prescription medications, and additional clinical parameters. Local institutional review boards approved the protocol at each site, and the trial was registered at https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ( NCT01038583 ) and https://www.isrctn.com (ISRCTN83772183). Complete details of ASPREE and its primary results have been previously published. 18

As part of the baseline and annual study visits, each participant had systolic and diastolic BP measured by trained study staff according to standard operating procedures. Participants were instructed to remove any upper arm garments, to allow for measurement of BP on the bare arm. The upper arm circumference was then measured to determine the appropriate cuff size. Following placement of the cuff, the participant was instructed to remain seated quietly, with back supported and feet flat on the floor for 5 min. The ASPREE protocol did not require a specific device model since it was not designed as a BP intervention study; however, all BP monitors used in the study were required to meet validation criteria from at least one of the following organizations: Association for the Advancement of Medical Instruments, British Hypertension Society, or European Society for Hypertension. In Australia, the Omron HEM‐790IT, HEM‐7203, 7121, and 7130 models were used, while in the US, the majority of sites used the Omron HEM‐907XL. Unless contraindicated, BP was measured using the left arm. The mean of three separate and consecutive readings 1 min apart was recorded as the BP for the study visit. BP was managed throughout the trial by the participant's usual care provider according to their accustomed care process. Participants were instructed to take their study drug (aspirin or matching placebo) at the same time every day. Participants who were taking antihypertensives did not receive any special instructions about timing of when to take their antihypertensives in relation to their ASPREE study visit.

Systolic and diastolic BP measurements for each participant at baseline and each annual visit through the completion of the randomized trial period were summarized using means and standard deviations. Additionally, means and standard deviations were used to summarize baseline characteristics on a continuous scale and relative proportions for baseline characteristics on a categorical scale. Where specified, variables on a continuous scale (e.g., age) were transformed into categorical groups. Characteristics at baseline were compared descriptively.

We used linear mixed effects models with random intercepts to evaluate the BP trajectories in the aspirin and placebo groups over each annual visit from baseline through the end of the randomized trial period to account for between and within‐individual variability of repeated BP readings over time. Separate linear mixed models were performed for systolic and diastolic BP. Analyses by several subgroups (e.g., elevated BP, normal BP, treated/untreated with antihypertensive medication, age, sex, chronic kidney disease [CKD], diabetes, frailty) were also explored with inclusion of interaction terms in the linear mixed models where appropriate.

We conducted an additional sensitivity analysis to examine incident treated hypertension occurring during the trial follow‐up in participants who were untreated at baseline. Those who were on antihypertensives or had elevated BP ≥140/90 mm Hg at baseline were excluded from the sensitivity analysis. This BP threshold was chosen as it reflected the accepted BP threshold for hypertension during the ASPREE randomized trial period. Since the BP at an annual visit could be transiently elevated but not indicative of a hypertension diagnosis, we defined incident hypertension as commencement of an antihypertensive medication (WHO ATC codes C02, C03 [excluding C03D], C07, C08, C09) occurring during the follow‐up period. Because antihypertensive medication use was recorded at annual visits, incident hypertension was considered an interval censored outcome (between annual visits), and analyzed with interval censored Cox proportional‐hazards regression. 19 Participants who did not reach the incident hypertension endpoint were right censored at the last annual visit, time of death or withdrawal, whichever occurred first. Standard errors were estimated using bootstrapping ( N = 500). Plots of the transformed survival function was used to verify the proportional hazards assumption.

All analyses were intention‐to‐treat. Mixed effects models were performed using STATA MP version 17.0, while interval censored Cox proportional‐hazards regression was performed in R version 4.3.1. 20 All statistical analyses were two‐sided using a 0.05 significance level and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated.
sections.results:
The ASPREE trial cohort included 19 114 participants, of whom 9525 were randomized to aspirin and 9589 randomized to placebo. Baseline participant demographic characteristics are presented in Table 1 and were well‐balanced between both groups. The mean age at randomization was 75.1 years; approximately 74.3% were hypertensive, about one quarter (24.8%) had CKD, and 10.7% had diabetes. Mean (SD) systolic and diastolic BPs at baseline were 139.2 (16.5) and 77.3 mm Hg (10.0), respectively. As reported previously, median follow‐up of the trial cohort during the randomized trial period was 4.7 years. 18

The mean systolic and diastolic BPs at each annual visit, as well as the mean number of antihypertensives taken, are summarized in Table 2 . The mean number of annual BP measurements per study participant (excluding baseline) through the duration of the trial was 3.7 (range: 0, 6) across both the aspirin and placebo groups. The number of participants with reported BP measurements decreased over time, largely reflecting the 4‐year window of participant recruitment between 2010 and 2014; however, the number of BP measures remained consistent between both groups throughout the annual visits. Likewise, the number of antihypertensives taken in both groups was similar throughout the study duration.

The overall population means for systolic and diastolic BPs in both the aspirin and placebo groups decreased throughout the trial period, from approximately 139/77 to 135/72 mm Hg (Figure 1 ). The estimates from the linear mixed effects models for yearly change in BP, along with the corresponding 95% CIs, are shown in Table 3 . In the placebo group, mean systolic BP was estimated to have decreased by 0.46 mm Hg (95% CI: −0.54, −0.39) and diastolic BP decreased by 0.72 mm Hg (95% CI: −0.77, −0.68) per year. Similarly, in the aspirin group, mean systolic BP was estimated to have decreased by 0.49 mm Hg (95% CI: −0.57, −0.42) and diastolic BP decreased by 0.77 mm Hg (95% CI: −0.82, −0.73) per year. The mean change in systolic BP was not different in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group (−0.03 mm Hg per year, 95% CI: −0.13, 0.07; p = .541). Likewise, the mean change in diastolic BP was not different in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group (−0.05 mm Hg per year, 95% CI: −0.11, 0.01; p = .094).

Abbreviations: BP, blood pressure; CI, confidence interval.

In the sensitivity analysis of incident treated hypertension in participants who did not have elevated BP and were not taking antihypertensives at baseline, 469/2470 (51.2%) of the aspirin‐treated participants commenced antihypertensives during the trial. This rate was similar to the 422/2449 (46.5%) randomized to placebo who commenced antihypertensives (HR for aspirin vs. placebo = 1.10, 95% CI 0.97, 1.26, p = .136).

Change in BP over time was further examined based on participants’ antihypertensive treatment status and BP level (normal or elevated) at baseline, as well as key baseline demographics and selected morbidities (Figure 2 , Tables S1–S6 ). The difference in BP change over time between the aspirin and placebo groups did not vary across these subgroups (interaction p ‐value > .05 for all), indicating no heterogeneity of treatment effects was present.

sections.discussion:
Despite prior research, several important questions about aspirin's effect on BP in older adults persist, such as the magnitude of BP change with aspirin, and whether effects vary based on underlying patient‐specific factors including age, level of BP, underlying comorbidities, and antihypertensive treatment status. In our post‐hoc analysis of 19 114 older adults enrolled in the ASPREE trial where BP was managed via usual care, we found no difference in the change in BP during follow‐up between those randomized to daily low‐dose aspirin or placebo. Moreover, there was no difference in the change in systolic or diastolic BP for aspirin compared with placebo in participants with or without elevated BP at baseline, and this did not differ according to whether they were receiving treatment with antihypertensive medication at baseline. These findings were also consistent across subgroups of demographics and comorbidities, including age, sex, CKD, diabetes, and frailty. Finally, rates of incident treated hypertension during in‐trial follow‐up for those whose BP < 140/90 mm Hg at baseline were similar between those randomized to aspirin and those randomized to placebo.

Aspirin is an important agent for secondary prevention of CVD. However, despite recent changes in guideline recommendations, it remains widely used even for primary prevention. 21 , 22 In older adults, the risk and prevalence of hypertension are increased, and it is important to clarify the effect of aspirin on BP in this population. Two prior meta‐analyses focused on NSAIDs included aspirin in doses ≥1.5 g/d and reported slight increases in BP in hypertensive patients, but did not separate the BP effect for aspirin from other NSAIDs. 3 , 4 A more recent meta‐analysis noted the lack of reliable evidence on whether taking aspirin affects BP. 23 In their analysis of five studies comprising 20 312 individuals, aspirin 75–100 mg/day did not significantly affect BP; however, the authors acknowledged significant heterogeneity in the included studies which were limited by small sample sizes, short follow‐ups (3 months or less), and lack of placebo controls.

Our finding of no effect of aspirin on BP in the hypertensive subgroup is consistent with prior intervention studies examining the effects of aspirin on BP in younger treated hypertensives. Nawarskas and coworkers found no significant effect of 2 weeks of assigned aspirin 81 or 325 mg in 17 hypertensive patients taking either enalapril or losartan. 12 Avanzini and coworkers studied 142 hypertensive patients (mean age 59 years) randomizing them to aspirin or placebo and examining clinic and 24 h ambulatory BP at baseline and 3 months, also reported no significant differences. 13 In the largest study, a post‐hoc analysis of the Hypertension Optimal Treatment trial of 18 790 hypertensives (mean age 61 years) randomized to 75 mg/d aspirin or placebo, systolic and diastolic BPs achieved with antihypertensive treatment were superimposable in aspirin and placebo‐treated patients. 11

Our findings extend these results with confidence into the older adult population, confirming that treatment status and level of BP do not modify low‐dose aspirin's effect on BP. Key strengths of our analysis include the underlying blinded randomization to aspirin or placebo, the large size of the ASPREE cohort and length of follow‐up, and the collection of standardized in‐trial BP measurements. Antihypertensive use in response to BP throughout the ASPREE trial was managed by the participant's usual care provider, providing a pragmatic feature that potential differences between aspirin and placebo in BP resulting from routine antihypertensive adjustments are likely to be highly generalizable to older adults. Additionally, the similar number of BP medications in both groups follow‐up suggests consistency in BP throughout the duration of the trial. Finally, we used linear‐mixed models to estimate the change in BP, which accounts for between and within‐individual variability in repeated measures over time rather than just examining mean differences in BP between the two groups at beginning and end of study for the overall trial cohort.

We acknowledge limitations of our study, which notably include the relatively healthy population and lack of ethnic diversity enrolled in ASPREE. Although hypertension was common, participants had to be free of documented CVD, and those with uncontrolled severe high BP were excluded. Thus, we cannot assume that aspirin has no effect on BP in those with highest cardiovascular risk, including very high BP, or those with significant cardiovascular morbidity taking aspirin for secondary prevention. Our findings, contextualized with that of prior research, lead us to believe it would be unlikely for low‐dose aspirin to affect BP in these subgroups. Other important limitations include lack of dose and frequency information for antihypertensives taken by the cohort, or use of antihypertensives for reasons other than BP control. Although the overall change in BP between groups, the risk of incident treated hypertension, and the mean number of antihypertensives throughout follow‐up were similar for aspirin and placebo‐randomized participants, it is possible that the antihypertensive regimens were adjusted differently between groups which may have minimized differences in BP change. Finally, our results pertain only to chronic low‐dose aspirin and should not be extrapolated to higher doses.
sections.conclusion: Hypertension is a common condition with aging. Aspirin is used both as a preventive and for managing pain and inflammation, which leads to substantial numbers of older adults being exposed to aspirin chronically. We conclude from the results of a large, long‐term randomized primary prevention trial of aspirin, that daily low‐dose aspirin does not significantly affect the level of BP or new onset treated hypertension in older adults when managed via usual care, regardless of underlying antihypertensive treatment status, BP control, or important demographics and morbidities.
